docs.title: agentkit
docs.text:
agentkit is a model-neutral Python framework for building agent harnesses. It has one model execution path: CallRuntime. AgentRunner composes agent instructions, context, tools, skills, delegation, and verification on top of that runtime.

The host application owns workflow orchestration, durable business state, and domain-specific grading. agentkit supplies the model call, tool loop, events, continuation, accounting, and hooks that a host can compose into its harness.

docs.title: The runtime and the harness
docs.text:
Use CallRuntime.ask() for a single request or CallRuntime.run() for a bounded tool loop. Use AgentRunner.run_agent() when you want agent definitions, minds, prompt composition, scoped tools, and memory providers. Both call the same runtime and return the same Answer and Usage contracts.

import asyncio

from agentkit.agents import AgentDefinition, AgentRunner, InstructionSet
from agentkit.core.runtime import CallRuntime
from agentkit.models import Binding, Mode, PriceTable


async def main() -> None:
    # Supply an adapter configured for the selected mode/model.
    adapter = ...  # A provider adapter configured for the selected model.
    async with CallRuntime(adapters={Mode.OPENAI_API: adapter}, pricing=PriceTable.default()) as runtime:
        runner = AgentRunner(runtime)
        answer = await runner.run_agent(
            AgentDefinition(
                id="assistant",
                version="1",
                description="Answer clearly and accurately.",
            ),
            InstructionSet("What does this service do?"),
            {},
            binding=Binding(Mode.OPENAI_API, "your-configured-model"),
            call_id="docs-example",
        )
        print(answer.text)


asyncio.run(main())

The package supports Anthropic API, OpenAI API, Claude Code CLI, and Codex CLI adapters. Runtime behavior belongs in the shared runtime; adapters translate provider requests and responses. Provider-specific capability limits are surfaced explicitly.

docs.title: What plugs into the harness
docs.text:
• Minds define reasoning strategy independently of model transport.
  • Tools are declared with side-effect metadata, validated, scoped, and dispatched by the current runtime path.
  • Context travels with messages and can be transformed by a context policy between slices or before resume.
  • Memory providers contribute untrusted context during prompt composition.
  • Skills provide approved resources and can emit lifecycle events.
  • EventHub exposes call and agent events to host subscribers. Subscribers can opt into isolated failure handling.
  • Pricing, limits, output validation, retries, and continuation are configured through the runtime call contract.

Runnable examples live under tests/examples; offline tests live under tests/source, and provider-backed evaluations live under tests/evals.

docs.title: Development checks
docs.text:
uv run pytest -q
uv run ruff check agentkit tests

Provider-backed checks are opt-in and documented in tests/evals/README.md. Their reports state which modes, models, and scenarios were actually exercised.

docs.text: Path Responsibility agentkit/agents Agent definitions, minds, prompt composition, and AgentRunner agentkit/core/runtime CallRuntime, call lifecycle, accounting, and events agentkit/models/providers/frontiers Direct API adapters agentkit/models/providers/cli Installed Claude Code and Codex CLI adapters agentkit/tools Tool definitions, execution, policy, and hosted tools agentkit/state/context Immutable working context, context policies, and memory providers tests/source Offline source and conformance tests tests/evals Opt-in real-provider evaluations tests/examples Runnable usage examples

docs.title: Publishing agentkit
docs.text: How releases work. Read this before your first release.

docs.title: PyPI distribution name
docs.text:
Distribution name: arc-agentkit (the string you pip install). Import name: agentkit (unchanged — every existing user of from agentkit import ... keeps working).

PyPI's namespace for agentkit is owned by a different unrelated project (vik@japanvik.net, "distributed llm agent swarms", v0.0.4 · Mar 2026). Reserving a brand-attributed name keeps discovery clean and preserves the import agentkit ergonomics.

The distinction is standard in Python packaging — e.g. pip install Django → import django, pip install python-dotenv → import dotenv.

docs.title: Release flow (once per version)
docs.text: We publish via PyPI Trusted Publisher (OIDC) — no long-lived PyPI API tokens live in the repo or in secrets. GitHub Actions signs a request to PyPI, PyPI verifies against the trusted-publisher configuration on the project page, and the release is uploaded. If you leaked a token, PyPI would issue a warning and revoke; with OIDC there's no token to leak.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. Register the distribution on TestPyPI first (dry-run environment):
  2. Go to https://test.pypi.org/manage/account/publishing/
  3. "Add a new publisher"
  4. Owner: arc-labs-ai
  5. Repository: agentkit
  6. Workflow name: release.yml

  7. Environment: pypi (matches the environment: block in release.yml)

  8. Same again for real PyPI:

  9. https://pypi.org/manage/account/publishing/

  10. Same shape.

  11. First-time publish will fail on PyPI until PyPI has a version of the package registered. Options: register the name via an initial dummy release from the maintainer's account (bootstrap), OR publish to TestPyPI first and then request PyPI reserve the name.

docs.title: Every release
docs.text:
1. Update CHANGELOG.md — new entry at the top under the new version number (semver). Format: ## [0.2.0] - 2026-XX-XX + bullet list of changes.
  2. Bump version in pyproject.toml. Semver: patch for bug fix, minor for backward-compatible feature, major for breaking change.
  3. Merge to main with the changelog + version bump.
  4. Tag the commit with v<version> (matching pyproject exactly):
git tag v0.2.0 && git push origin v0.2.0
  1. GitHub Actions release.yml fires on the tag:
  2. Builds wheel + sdist via hatchling.
  3. Runs twine check dist/* to catch metadata errors before upload.
  4. Requests OIDC token, publishes to PyPI.

  5. Creates a GitHub Release with generated notes.

  6. Verify on PyPI (~2 minutes after publish):

pip install --upgrade arc-agentkit
python -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('arc-agentkit'))"

docs.title: Local dry-run before tagging
docs.text:
Always run this before creating the tag:

make build          # hatchling → dist/*.whl + dist/*.tar.gz
make publish-dry    # twine check dist/*

If publish-dry complains about long-description rendering, README markdown, or invalid classifiers — fix those in the same commit as the changelog and version bump. Failing publishes leave dead space on the version list.

docs.title: SemVer policy
docs.text:
We're pre-1.0 (currently 0.x). Rules we hold:

  • Patch (0.x.PATCH) — bug fixes, docs, internal refactors that don't change the public API's behavior.
  • Minor (0.MINOR.0) — new public API surface OR intentional behavior changes to existing API surface. Log in CHANGELOG under "Changed" / "Deprecated" / "Removed" sections.
  • Major (MAJOR.0.0) — reserved for the 1.0 stabilization pass and any subsequent hard-breaking rewrites.

Public API = anything exported from agentkit/__init__.py or a top-level subpackage's __init__.py. Anything under _private.py or prefixed with _ is fair game to change in a patch release.

docs.title: Yanking a bad release
docs.text:
If a release ships broken:

pip install --upgrade twine
twine yank arc-agentkit 0.2.0 --reason "critical bug in X — use 0.2.1"

Yanking hides the version from pip install arc-agentkit (unbounded) but leaves pip install arc-agentkit==0.2.0 working for anyone who pinned it. Then ship the fixed version.

Never delete a released version. PyPI enforces this — deletions break downstream lockfiles for anyone who pinned to the yanked version.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
• Trusted publisher misconfigured → 403 on upload. Check that the workflow file name in the publisher config matches release.yml exactly.
  • Wheel builds but sdist doesn't → hatchling's [tool.hatch.build] didn't include a source file. Add it to packages or include.
  • twine check warns about README → PyPI parses the README as reStructuredText by default. We set readme = "README.md" and PyPI handles the text/markdown content-type via content_type inference from the file extension. Make sure the content_type metadata field is set to text/markdown in the built wheel's METADATA.
  • Version mismatch between tag and pyproject.toml → CI fails early. Fix the mismatch before re-tagging.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
The authoritative guide lives at the repository root:

  • CONTRIBUTING.md — full contributor guide.
  • CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md — the community standards we hold each other to.
  • CHANGELOG.md — release notes.

docs.title: Quick pointers
docs.text:
• Bug reports and feature requests — open an issue on GitHub.
  • Design changes — start a discussion before opening a large PR, especially for anything touching the kernel, the middleware contract, or an agent Protocol.
  • Docs improvements — edit files under docs/ and open a PR; the "Edit this page" link at the top of every page takes you there directly.

docs.title: Local docs preview
docs.text:
uv pip install mkdocs-material 'mkdocstrings[python]' mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized-plugin
uv run mkdocs serve

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000.
